rationale: A wins because it keeps the sharp ideas tied to the facts instead of spending money it does not have. Its best line, "What Substack's $400M creator number says about Substack's own revenue," turns the disclosure into a reporter's math problem while admitting the math needs definitions. B has real instincts, but "the same cut now extending over video and podcast monetization" and "short on funding" are unsupported leaps; that's how a decent angle becomes a correction.
gaps_in_A: "Substack is done being a newsletter company" is punchy, but a little over-declared. Without an on-record strategy quote, this should stay framed as a category question, not a settled identity change.
"Draft the category angle first" is defensible, but it underplays the chance that pinning down the $400M definition first could produce the sharper business story.

"The concern becomes concrete the moment writers see video in their subscribers' feeds" is plausible, but it quietly assumes how the feed appears to subscribers. Ask it as a distribution-ranking question unless Substack has shown that UI.
gaps_in_B: "the same cut now extending over video and podcast monetization" is not in the update. The facts say 10% of subscription revenue; they do not say video and podcast monetization carry the identical cut.
"short on funding" overstates "public funding struggles." Those are not the same thing, and a finance reporter will notice before lunch.
"capital-intensive infrastructure" may be a fair question, but B states it too confidently without knowing whether Substack built video hosting itself, used a partner, or how material the cost is.
"the YouTube/Patreon/Substack competitive set" imports competitors the facts did not name. B later warns against this, which makes the earlier slip worse, not better.
